propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of Immigration Officer's refusal of Permanent Residence on H&C grounds under section 25(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Pritam Singh Shah, seeks judicial review of the decision of an Immigration Officer [the Officer], dated November 15, 2018, which refused his Application for Permanent Residence from within Canada on Humanitarian and Compassionate [H&C] grounds, pursuant to section 25(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 [the Act].

paragraphs.summary: Applicant seeks judicial review of Immigration Officer's refusal of Permanent Residence on H&C grounds under section 25(1) of the Act, court states.

propositions.text: Application is dismissed; court sympathizes but must assess reasonableness of Officer's decision.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the Application is dismissed. While the Court sympathizes with the Applicant’s circumstances and his desire to remain in Canada with his family, the Court’s role is not to make the decision, rather to determine if the Officer’s decision is reasonable.

propositions.text: Officer's decision is reasonable, justified, transparent, intelligible, and defensible in law and facts.
propositions.quote: The Court finds that the decision is reasonable; it is justified, transparent and intelligible and is defensible in accordance with the law and the facts on the record.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses application, sympathizes with applicant, but finds Officer's decision reasonable, justified, transparent, and defensible.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah is 78, Indian citizen, with family in Canada who arrived in 2010 and are permanent residents.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah is a 78-year-old citizen of India. His only family ‒ his son, daughter-in-law and two grandsons ‒ arrived in Canada in 2010 and are now permanent residents.

propositions.text: Before 2010, Mr. Shah lived with family in India and helped raise grandchildren, imparting culture and language.
propositions.quote: Prior to 2010 Mr. Shah lived with his family in India. He attests that his family is very close and that he helped raise his grandchildren, imparting his traditional culture and language.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah is 78 Indian citizen with family in Canada since 2010; he lived in India before and helped raise grandchildren, court states.

propositions.text: Daughter-in-law and youngest grandson returned to India after 2010 to care for Mr. Shah; caretaker neglected him causing isolation and poor health.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah recounts that his daughter-in-law and youngest grandson returned to India shortly after their arrival in Canada in 2010 to care for him. Before returning to Canada in 2012, Mr. Shah’s daughter-in-law arranged for a caretaker for Mr. Shah. He attests that the caretaker neglected him, leaving him in isolation and poor mental and physical health.

paragraphs.summary: Daughter-in-law and grandson returned to India to care for Mr. Shah; caretaker neglected him causing isolation and poor health, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah obtained a multiple entry TRV in 2015 valid until 2025, allowing stays up to six months with extensions.
propositions.quote: On March 26, 2015, he obtained a multiple entry Temporary Residence Visa [TRV], which expires on January 13, 2025. This multiple entry TRV permits Mr. Shah to remain in Canada for periods of up to six months with possible extensions.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah obtained multiple entry TRV in 2015 valid until 2025 allowing six-month stays, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah entered Canada as visitor in April 2017 and applied for Permanent Residence on H&C grounds in June 2017 citing establishment, family ties, separation impact, frail health, and best interests of grandsons.
propositions.quote: In April 2017, Mr. Shah entered Canada as a visitor. On June 15, 2017, Mr. Shah applied for Permanent Residence from within Canada on H&C grounds, noting in particular: his establishment in Canada, family ties, the impact of separation from his family, his frail health and the best interest of his grandsons.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah entered Canada in 2017 and applied for Permanent Residence on H&C grounds citing establishment, family ties, separation, health, and grandsons' best interests.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah arrived again in Canada in February 2018 and has remained due to TRV extension.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah arrived in Canada again in February 2018 and has remained since due to the extension of his TRV.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah arrived again in Canada in 2018 and stayed due to TRV extension, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah’s family submitted online interest to sponsor him in 2017 but was not selected; another attempt in 2019 failed due to program closure.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah’s family in Canada also submitted online “an interest to sponsor a family member or grandparent” in 2017 but their application was not selected. In January 2019, Mr. Shah’s son attempted to file another online interest, but the program closed due to high volume before he could do so.

paragraphs.summary: Family tried to sponsor Mr. Shah online in 2017 and 2019 but was unsuccessful, court states.

propositions.text: Officer considered evidence and factors, noted positives but found H&C exemption not justified on global assessment.
propositions.quote: The Officer considered the relevant evidence and factors. The Officer noted that there were several positive factors but, based on his global assessment, found that an H&C exemption was not justified.

paragraphs.summary: Officer considered evidence, noted positives, but found H&C exemption not justified on global assessment, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer gave positive weight to Mr. Shah’s visits and compliance with immigration regulations.
propositions.quote: With respect to Mr. Shah’s establishment in Canada, the Officer noted that Mr. Shah had visited Canada several times and gave positive weight to the fact that Mr. Shah had always complied with Canadian immigration regulations and had returned to India when required.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave positive weight to Mr. Shah's visits and compliance with immigration rules, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Shah’s investments and pension enabling independent living in India and son’s support if needed.
propositions.quote: The Officer noted that Mr. Shah had some investments and a monthly pension that would enable him to live independently in India. The Officer also noted that Mr. Shah’s son would support him if needed whether he returned to India or remained in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted Mr. Shah’s investments, pension, and son’s support for independent living in India, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer gave little weight to Mr. Shah’s continuous residence in Canada since February 2018 as establishment factor.
propositions.quote: The Officer noted that Mr. Shah has resided with his family in Canada continuously since February 2018, but gave little weight to his time spent in Canada as a factor supporting his establishment.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave little weight to Mr. Shah’s residence in Canada since 2018 as establishment factor, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer gave significant positive weight to Mr. Shah’s family relationship and acknowledged no relatives in India.
propositions.quote: The Officer gave significant positive weight to Mr. Shah’s relationship with his family. The Officer acknowledged that Mr. Shah had no relatives in India and that his only family is his son, daughter-in-law and grandsons in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave significant positive weight to Mr. Shah’s family ties and lack of relatives in India, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer gave little weight to family separation impact due to lack of corroborative evidence of need for support.
propositions.quote: The Officer gave little weight to the impact of family separation. The Officer found that there was little corroborative evidence to explain why Mr. Shah was not capable of living on his own and required day-to-day support or assistance.

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Shah passed medical exam for TRV extension and had multiple entry visa valid until 2025 allowing visits.
propositions.quote: The Officer noted that Mr. Shah had recently passed the medical examination to permit his TRV to be extended. The Officer added that Mr. Shah’s multiple entry visa, valid until 2025, would permit him to continue to visit his family in Canada and noted that there was little evidence to suggest that he is not fit to travel or would experience difficulty doing so.

propositions.text: Officer noted little evidence that Mr. Shah would be unable to return to India based on age.
propositions.quote: The Officer also noted that there was little evidence that he would not be able to return to India based on his age.

paragraphs.summary: Officer gave little weight to family separation impact, noted medical exam passed, multiple entry visa, and no evidence Mr. Shah can't return to India, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer noted oldest grandson (19) does not meet definition of 'child' for BIOC analysis.
propositions.quote: With respect to the best interests of the children affected [BIOC] ‒ i.e., Mr. Shah’s grandsons ‒ the Officer noted that the oldest grandson was 19 years of age and did not meet the definition of “child” for the purposes of the BIOC analysis.

paragraphs.summary: Officer noted oldest grandson is 19 and not a 'child' for BIOC analysis, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer found little evidence of Mr. Shah’s role in younger grandson’s life; basic needs met without him.
propositions.quote: With respect to Mr. Shah’s 17-year-old grandson, the Officer found that there was little evidence of Mr. Shah’s role in his younger grandson’s life. The Officer concluded that the grandson’s basic medical, educational, and social needs would continue to be met in Mr. Shah’s absence.

paragraphs.summary: Officer found little evidence of Mr. Shah’s role in younger grandson’s life; needs met without him, court reports.

propositions.text: Officer concluded H&C factors globally did not warrant exemption under subsection 25(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: In conclusion, the Officer found that the H&C factors, assessed globally, did not warrant an exemption under subsection 25(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Officer concluded H&C factors globally did not warrant exemption under subsection 25(1), court reports.

propositions.text: Mr. Shah argues decision is unreasonable; Officer failed to consider whole evidence and ignored relevant evidence on grandson’s best interests.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that the decision is not reasonable: the Officer erred by failing to consider the evidence of his circumstances as a whole in relation to the hardships he would face if required to return to India; and, the Officer erred in his assessment of the best interests of his younger grandson, by ignoring relevant evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues decision is unreasonable due to failure to consider all evidence and ignoring relevant evidence on grandson’s best interests.

propositions.text: Standard of review for Officer’s H&C decision is reasonableness (Kanthasamy at para 44).
propositions.quote: The jurisprudence has clearly established that the standard of review of an Officer’s decision with respect to an H&C application is reasonableness (Kanthasamy v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61, [2015] 3 SCR 909 [Kanthasamy] at para 44).

paragraphs.summary: Standard of review for Officer’s H&C decision is reasonableness, per Kanthasamy, court states.

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensibility within facts and law (Dunsmuir at para 47).
propositions.quote: To determine whether a decision is reasonable, the Court looks for “the existence of justification, transparency and intelligibility within the decision-making process” and considers “whether the decision falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and law” (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47, [2008] 1 SCR 190).

paragraphs.summary: Reasonableness requires justification, transparency, intelligibility, and defensibility within facts and law, per Dunsmuir, court states.

propositions.text: The Court must defer to the decision-maker and intervene only if the decision fails the Dunsmuir standard.
propositions.quote: The role of the Court is not to remake the decision or to reweigh the evidence. The Court owes deference to the decision-maker and should only intervene where the decision does not reflect the Dunsmuir standard.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states it must defer to the decision-maker and intervene only if the decision fails the Dunsmuir standard.

propositions.text: The H&C Officer failed to consider relevant evidence of hardship from his unique circumstances including family dependency and lack of social network in India.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that the H&C Officer failed to consider relevant evidence of the hardship he would face resulting from his unique circumstances, including his emotional and physical dependency on his family in Canada, his lack of a social network in India, and his inability to create new networks due to his advanced age.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer failed to consider hardship evidence related to his family dependency and social isolation in India.

propositions.text: Age and family dependency are important factors in assessing hardship, supported by cited cases Makarenko and Epstein.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that his age and family dependency are important factors that should be considered in assessing hardship (Makarenko v Canada...; Epstein v Canada...).

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues age and family dependency are important hardship factors, citing Makarenko and Epstein.

propositions.text: The Officer did not consider evidence holistically, instead considered factors in segments causing contradictory findings, contrary to Kanthasamy.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah further submits that the Officer did not consider the evidence holistically, contrary to the principle in Kanthasamy at para 113. [He argues that the Officer considered the factors in segments which led to contradictory findings.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer failed holistic evidence consideration, causing contradictory findings, contrary to Kanthasamy.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to follow Baker's guidance to consider children's best interests with substantial weight in BIOC analysis.
propositions.quote: With respect to the Officer’s BIOC analysis, Mr. Shah submits that the Officer did not follow the guidance of the Supreme Court of Canada in Baker... requiring decision-makers to “consider children’s best interests as an important factor, give them substantial weight, and be alert, alive and sensitive to them.”

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer failed to follow Baker's guidance on children's best interests in BIOC analysis.

propositions.text: The Officer ignored evidence of Mr. Shah's relationship with his younger grandson, including photos and a letter from older grandson.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah submits that the Officer ignored relevant evidence of his relationship with his younger grandson... failed to consider the photographs... and the letter written by his older grandson... failed to draw reasonable inferences from his older grandson’s description.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer ignored evidence of his relationship with his younger grandson and failed to draw reasonable inferences.

propositions.text: The Officer focused on irrelevant BIOC factors like grandson’s access to Canadian services, ignoring other relevant factors.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah also submits that the Officer failed to take into account other relevant BIOC factors, focussing instead on irrelevant factors, including his grandson’s access to the Canadian medical system, education system and social services.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer focused on irrelevant BIOC factors, ignoring other relevant ones.

propositions.text: H&C considerations are no longer assessed by underserved and disproportionate hardships; Officer applied Kanthasamy principles and assessed all relevant factors globally.
propositions.quote: The Respondent notes that H&C considerations are no longer assessed through the lens of underserved and disproportionate hardships. The Officer did not err by failing to specifically address hardship, rather the Officer applied the principles of Kanthasamy and assessed all the relevant H&C factors.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer properly applied Kanthasamy and assessed all relevant H&C factors globally.

propositions.text: Officer noted positive factors like family ties but found little evidence for other claims; multiple entry visa supports travel to Canada.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Officer noted several positive factors, including Mr. Shah’s strong family ties, but found a lack of evidence to support Mr. Shah’s other submissions... The Respondent notes that the Officer observed that the multiple entry visa, valid until 2025, permits Mr. Shah to travel to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent says the Officer noted family ties but found little evidence for other claims; visa allows travel to Canada.

propositions.text: Officer correctly stated law on BIOC, found older grandson not a child, reasonably assessed younger grandson’s best interests.
propositions.quote: With respect to the BIOC, the Respondent submits that the Officer correctly stated the law... and reasonably assessed the BIOC of the younger grandson.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent argues the Officer correctly applied BIOC law and reasonably assessed the younger grandson’s best interests.

propositions.text: The Officer’s decision is reasonable, addressing all relevant factors and evidence, with weight within discretion; Court will not reweigh evidence.
propositions.quote: The Officer did not err in his analysis of the H&C application... The Officer addressed all of the factors relevant to the H&C application and all of the evidence submitted... The weight attached to the considerations is within the Officer’s discretion and the Court’s role is not to reweigh the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer’s decision reasonable, addressing all factors and evidence, with weight within discretion.

propositions.text: Section 25 allows discretionary exemption from Act criteria on humanitarian and compassionate grounds, considering best interests of affected child.
propositions.quote: Section 25 of the Act... may be granted on the basis of humanitarian and compassionate considerations, “taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected”.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states section 25 allows discretionary exemption on humanitarian and compassionate grounds considering a child's best interests.

propositions.text: H&C exemption is discretionary, exceptional relief; onus on applicant to prove entitlement with sufficient evidence; officers must consider all evidence.
propositions.quote: This exemption is discretionary and exceptional relief... The onus is at all times on an applicant to establish with sufficient evidence... Officers who conduct H&C assessments must consider all of the evidence presented and be satisfied that relief is justified.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains H&C relief is discretionary, exceptional, with onus on applicant to prove entitlement; officers must consider all evidence.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy explains relief under section 25 varies depending on facts and context of each case.
propositions.quote: In Kanthasamy, the Supreme Court explained that what will warrant relief under section 25 will vary depending on the facts and context of each case (at para 25).

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy explains section 25 relief varies with facts and context of each case.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy calls for liberal interpretation of H&C, weighing all relevant facts; some hardship is inevitable and alone insufficient for relief.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court also emphasized... the need to consider and weigh all relevant facts and factors and called for a more liberal interpretation of H&C considerations... some hardship is inevitable: [23] There will inevitably be some hardship... This alone will not generally be sufficient to warrant relief...

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy calls for liberal H&C interpretation weighing all facts; some hardship is inevitable and insufficient alone for relief.

propositions.text: Officer considered and weighed all relevant H&C factors, gave significant positive weight to family ties, but found little evidence for other claims.
propositions.quote: The decision conveys that the Officer considered and weighed all the relevant H&C factors. The Officer noted Mr. Shah’s dependency on his family and gave “significant positive weight” to his family ties... there was little evidence to explain why he is unable to live on his own...

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer considered all relevant H&C factors, gave weight to family ties, but found little evidence for other claims.

propositions.text: Officer did not consider factors in isolation or make contradictory findings; findings on family ties and establishment are consistent and supported.
propositions.quote: Contrary to Mr. Shah’s submissions, the Officer did not consider the relevant H&C factors in isolation or in segments and did not make contradictory findings... Both findings are supported by the evidence and are not inconsistent.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer did not consider factors in isolation or make contradictory findings; findings are consistent and supported.

propositions.text: Officer noted Mr. Shah’s age throughout decision and informed assessment; circumstances differ from Makarenko where age was ignored.
propositions.quote: Contrary to Mr. Shah’s submissions, his circumstances differ from those in Makarenko... the Officer noted Mr. Shah’s age at the outset... The Officer’s assessment... was informed by Mr. Shah’s personal circumstances, including his age.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer considered Mr. Shah’s age throughout, unlike in Makarenko where age was ignored.

propositions.text: Unlike Epstein, here Officer found little evidence of dependency or inability to care for self, re-establish, or travel.
propositions.quote: With respect to Mr. Shah’s reliance on Epstein... In the present case, the Officer repeatedly noted that there was little evidence to support the claims that Mr. Shah could not care for himself, re-establish himself in India or travel back and forth to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds that unlike Epstein, here the Officer found little evidence supporting dependency or inability to care for self or travel.

propositions.text: Officer acknowledged some hardship from family separation but noted some hardship is inevitable and alone does not warrant H&C relief.
propositions.quote: The Officer acknowledged that Mr. Shah would experience some hardship arising from the separation from his family, but as noted in Kanthasamy at para 23, some hardship is inevitable and does not, on its own, warrant H&C relief.

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the Officer acknowledged some hardship but noted it is inevitable and alone insufficient for H&C relief.

propositions.text: Kanthasamy requires assessing BIOC in H&C applications with well-identified and examined interests.
propositions.quote: In Kanthasamy, the Supreme Court of Canada (citing Baker at paras 74-75) reiterated the importance of assessing the BIOC in the context of an H&C application and noted that it is not enough to simply state that the interests have been considered. The child’s best interests must be well identified and examined in light of all the evidence (Kanthasamy, at para 39).

paragraphs.summary: Kanthasamy requires assessing the child's best interests in H&C applications with well-identified and examined interests, as the Supreme Court stated.

propositions.text: The Officer was alert, alive and sensitive to the younger grandson’s best interests and assessed BIOC in light of evidence.
propositions.quote: I do not agree with Mr. Shah’s submission that the Officer was not “alert, alive and sensitive” to his younger grandson’s best interests. Clearly the Officer assessed the BIOC in light of the evidence presented.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer was alert and sensitive to the younger grandson's best interests and assessed BIOC properly.

propositions.text: The Officer used an appropriate BIOC approach: establish interests, assess compromise, determine weight in H&C application.
propositions.quote: The Officer set out an appropriate approach to a BIOC analysis in the context of an H&C application; first, to establish what is in the child’s best interests; second, to determine the degree to which those interests would be compromised by one decision over the other; and, finally, to determine the weight that should be attached to the BIOC in the overall H&C application.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer used an appropriate approach to BIOC analysis in H&C applications, as the court finds.

propositions.text: The Officer found younger grandson’s best interests include being with parents and having basic needs met, noting little evidence.
propositions.quote: The Officer followed that approach, determining that the best interests of the younger grandson are to be around his parents and to have his basic needs met, including education, medical care, and social support from family and friends. The Officer addressed the evidence that was before him, noting that there was little.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found the younger grandson's best interests include being with parents and basic needs met, noting little evidence.

propositions.text: The Officer considered evidence of close relationship between Mr. Shah and grandson, including photographs over years.
propositions.quote: Contrary to Mr. Shah’s submission, the Officer considered the evidence submitted to support the close relationship between Mr. Shah and his grandson, including the photographs of the two together over the years. The Officer expressly referred to the “photos taken with Sahil and Karan [the grandsons] at varies [sic] stages of Karan’s life”.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer considered evidence of Mr. Shah's close relationship with his grandson, including photographs, contrary to Mr. Shah's submission.

propositions.text: The Officer acknowledged Mr. Shah lived with younger grandson most of his life and gave positive weight to family ties.
propositions.quote: The Officer also clearly acknowledged that Mr. Shah had lived with his younger grandson for most of his grandson’s life. In addition, the Officer gave significant positive weight to family ties, which also acknowledged the relationship he had with his grandsons.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer acknowledged Mr. Shah lived with his younger grandson and gave positive weight to family ties.

propositions.text: The Officer should have relied on older grandson’s letter to infer same relationship with younger grandson and negative impact.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah’s argument that the Officer should have relied on the letter from his older grandson, which described their particular relationship, to infer that the same relationship existed with his younger grandson and that his younger grandson’s interests would be negatively impacted,

propositions.text: The onus is on Mr. Shah to establish H&C considerations; Officer not required to infer younger grandson’s negative impact from older grandson’s letter.
propositions.quote: ignores the principle that the onus is on Mr. Shah to establish that H&C considerations justify the exemption from the requirements of the Act. The Officer was not required to read between the lines or draw an inference that the younger grandson’s best interests would be negatively affected. The letter from the older grandson did not even mention the younger grandson.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues the Officer should infer negative impact from older grandson’s letter; court finds onus on Mr. Shah and Officer not required to infer.

propositions.text: Officer focused on irrelevant factors like medical care and education, ignoring grandson’s age and Mr. Shah’s role.
propositions.quote: Mr. Shah’s argument that the Officer focussed on irrelevant factors, such as the availability of medical care and education for his grandson, yet ignored relevant factors such as his grandson’s age and the role played by Mr. Shah in his grandson’s life and cultural education is without merit.

propositions.text: Officer considered Guidelines factors, noted grandson’s age, and found little evidence younger grandson’s needs unmet without Mr. Shah.
propositions.quote: The Officer considered the factors set out in the Guidelines to the extent that they applied. The Officer clearly noted the grandson’s age. The Officer noted that – other than the photographs and the letters which described that they had all previously lived together ‒ there was little evidence that the younger grandson’s needs would not be met by his family in Canada, even in Mr. Shah’s absence.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Shah argues Officer focused on irrelevant factors; court finds Officer considered relevant factors and noted little evidence needs unmet.

propositions.text: Officer’s decision is justified, transparent, intelligible; exemption from Act not warranted; other options exist for Mr. Shah.
propositions.quote: In conclusion, the Officer’s decision is justified, transparent and intelligible. While sympathetic to the plight of Mr. Shah and his desire to remain with his family in Canada, the Officer reasonably found that an exemption from the requirements of the Act was not warranted. The Officer noted other options that Mr. Shah could pursue, including another online interest to sponsor or an application for the Parent and Grandparent Super Visa.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer’s decision is justified and exemption not warranted; other options exist for Mr. Shah.
